item.title: In Memory of Maria “Pola” Amaya
item.description:
Maria “Pola” Amaya, born July 23, 1935, beloved wife, mother, grandmother, and great grandmother passed away peacefully at her home surrounded by her loving family on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. She was born in Praxedis, Chih, Mexico to Manuel Rivera and Mariana Meza.

Pola was a devoted member of the Immaculate Conception Catholic Church. She was a homemaker, and in her younger years, had been a school teacher in Mexico and a live-in nanny in California. She was a woman of deep faith, loving, kind, and hardworking. Her favorite pastimes were spending time with her family, traveling, doing word-search puzzles, drawing, playing Loteria Mexican bingo, the casino, sewing, reading, and watching television game shows. Her most recent trips were to Texas, Florida, and Alaska.

Pola is survived by her daughters, Josefina "Josie" Amaya, Ana Hogue (husband John), and Maricruz "Mari" Morse (husband Richard); grandchildren, Mario Sena (wife Sky), Tanya Sena (wife Karis), Jackie LaBonte Carter (husband Gerren), Jennifer LaBonte Labayen (husband Laurence), Justin Morse, Jacob Morse; great grandchildren: Jayla, Deion, and Matthew Carter; Abigail, Madison, and Camille Labayen; Brooklyn, Zeb, and Emmie Sena; Wrenley and Keston Sena. She is also survived by her sister, Juanita Lopez; cousin, Socorro Garcia; numerous nieces and nephews.

Pola was preceded in death by her husband, Silvestre Amaya, of over 60 years in marriage; 13 siblings.

Pola’s daughters would like to send their gratitude and appreciation for the prayers, visits, food, flowers, and sympathy cards.

Services for Pola will be held on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at Immaculate Conception Catholic Church, 705 Delaware Ave, Alamogordo, New Mexico. Viewing will be held at 9:30 am with Rosary recited at 10:00 am. The Funeral Mass will be celebrated at 10:30 am. Pola will be laid to rest at 2:00 pm following the Mass at Mount Carmel Cemetery, 401 S. Zaragoza Rd, El Paso, Texas.

Pallbearers include John Hogue, Richard Morse, Justin Morse, Jacob Morse, Jayla Carter, Deion Carter, Matthew Carter, Gerren Carter, and Laurence Labayen.

item.title: In Memory of Alejandro “Hano” Morales
item.description:

item.title: In Loving Memory of Joseph “Jody” Mancillas
item.description:
Joseph “Jody” Mancillas, age 55, passed away peacefully on September 18, 2026. He leaves behind a legacy of warmth, kindness, and deeply cherished memories with everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.

One of Jody's greatest accomplishments was his dedicated career working at The Lodge at Cloudcroft for 35 years. It was truly his pride and joy, a place where he built lasting connections and left an undeniable impact through his decades of hard work and commitment.

Jody was a devoted son, brother, and friend who saw the world through a lens of appreciation and joy. In his younger years, he was happiest out on the court, playing basketball alongside his good friends. He loved bowling with his friends; he always brought a spirited energy to the lanes and thoroughly enjoyed the fun of a friendly competition. His love for local athletics continued throughout his life, and he always thoroughly enjoyed playing in local golf scrambles as well as dedicating his time line judging at high school volleyball tournaments.

Jody thoroughly enjoyed his extensive collection of music and movies, and he spent countless hours sharing his talent for baking, creating delicious desserts for both the staff and guests at The Lodge as well as for his beloved family and friends. He also held a deep, lifelong love for trains, and one of his favorite simple pleasures was listening to the train pass by.

Above all, Jody spent many hours on his photography, which was truly the biggest part of his life outside of work. He spent his happiest days hiking through nature, finding hidden beauty in everything around him and capturing it to share with the world. He also enjoyed memorable nights playing cards with the Turner family. Even during his illness, Jody brought people together, sharing lots of laughter, and he absolutely loved playing Farkle.

Known for his generous heart, he brought steady comfort and joy to those around him. His presence will be profoundly missed, but his memory will live on forever in the hearts of those he loved so dearly.

He is survived by his beloved mother, Sherry Crosson (husband Tim), and his brother, Jonathan Mancillas, along with a large, loving family of aunts, uncles, and cousins who will carry his strength and laughter forward. He is preceded in death by his father, Joseph L. Mancillas; his grandparents, Lucas and Angelita Mancillas; and his grandmother, Ruth A. Williams.

Family and friends are invited to gather to honor Jody's life and journey home. Services will be held on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, at Sacred Heart Mission Catholic Church (205 James Canyon Hwy).

• 11:00 AM | Mass of Christian Burial

• 2:05 PM | Celebration of Life Reception at The Pavilion at The Lodge Resort & Spa (199 Curlew)

item.title: Tularosa Trustees Delay Employee Raises Until Finance Director Can Attend
item.description:
TULAROSA, N.M. — The Tularosa Board of Trustees put off votes on a slate of village employee raises at a special meeting this week, after trustees said they could not weigh the budget impact without the village finance director in the room.

The board agreed to reconvene Monday at 6 p.m., when the mayor said the finance director would attend with figures. No raises were approved.

During public comment, Vivian Lewis told trustees she had learned of the special meeting only that Monday. She said a raise the municipal judge requested for her at earlier budget hearings was already written into the court's budget, which took effect July 1, but she had not received it.

The village's legal adviser, identified at the meeting as Nan, said a raise inside an approved budget does not need a new vote. If the employee was told the raise would start with the new fiscal year, she said, the employee is entitled to it from that date.

Asked whether the roughly $2-an-hour difference owed since July 1 should come as a supplemental check, the adviser deferred to the finance officer, saying a lump sum or an adjusted paycheck would both work.

The raises followed employee performance evaluations submitted by department heads. The police chief told trustees she had turned in her evaluations early and asked for raises, but they were left out of her department's budget. Police spending makes up more than half the village budget, she said, and "runs a little tight."

The mayor said the raises would come from each department's own budget, not the general fund. Several trustees pushed back, saying the raises were never budgeted and that they had raised the issue before the budget was adopted.

One trustee estimated that approving every raise on the agenda would add about $55,000, against roughly $170,000 the village has available. "We're not against giving raises," the trustee said, but the board needs to know where the money comes from.

Another trustee noted that some line items had already reached 157% of their budget two months into the fiscal year. He said he had asked at the prior meeting for the finance director, Valerie, to attend and had been assured she would. The mayor said she was unavailable.

The legal adviser told the board it first had to make a policy call: whether the raises would be paid from the general fund or from department budgets. Without the finance director, she said, that question was hard to answer.

Raises that fit inside a department's existing budget could proceed without further action, she said. Raises that don't would require a budget adjustment resolution once approved.

The mayor proposed setting aside the police chief's requests and voting on departments that could cover their own raises, including the utility supervisor, the senior center director and Clerk Garcia's three requests. But the clerk said she was willing to wait "because I don't think it's fair for everybody else." The board then agreed to hold all the raises until Monday.

With time left before adjourning, a trustee raised questions about specific public works wages. She said two employees, Nathan and Brett, took on new duties at the water plant without a wage change. She suggested extra pay for Brett, the department's only backup commercial driver's license holder, so the trash route can run when the regular driver is out.

Staff said Brett already earns trash-truck-driver pay for hours he drives, but nothing extra for holding the CDL. The adviser noted that such pay is the supervisor's call. The supervisor also confirmed an error in one employee's proposed raise, which will be corrected to $2, and said she would like to give part-time worker Carlos a $2 raise after a strong evaluation.

The utility supervisor reported the village reservoir at 36.5 feet as of that morning. The village is not drawing from it because of recent rain.

The board meets again Monday at 6 p.m. to take up the raises.

item.title: Vote Early Rally Oct 17, 2026 No Kings Committee
item.description:
The Republican Party, at the insistence of President Trump, is working hard to make it as difficult as possible for the average American to vote in the upcoming mid-term election. The Save Act, gerrymandering activities in many red states, large cities reducing the number of polling places in low-income areas, and the continuous lawsuits and appeals by the Administration to stop mail-in voting. There is a lot of reason to be concerned about the safety of your vote this mid-term election.

No Kings, Indivisible and 50501, along with others, are part of a nationwide coalition of pro-democracy organizations that have announced a nationwide No Kings Day Early Voting event for October 17, 2026. Local organizers at Democracy Otero County are supporting this effort for Otero County.

A Vote Early rally on October 17, 2026, from 9:00 AM to 11:00 AM at the intersection of White Sands Blvd. and 10th Street has been scheduled. You can sign up for this event at https://www.nokings.org.

Organizers ask that you register so that they can document attendance and to help them with planning, but registration is not required to attend the event.

Local organizers describe this as a celebration of the power of the people to dictate the destiny of our nation and our lives. When the rally winds down at 11:00 the plan is that everyone move, en masse, to the Otero County Fairgrounds to cast their votes, showing that the citizens of Otero County want a change from the trajectory we have been suffering through for the last two years.

Local activists, those folks you’ve seen rallying at the corner of White Sands Blvd. and Tenth Street for the last two years, will be out on that day, between 9:00 AM and 11:00 AM. They ask that you join them in sending this message to the Trump Administration: our voices will be heard; our votes will be counted. Group organizers say they have extra signs but encourage you to make your voice heard by creating your own message. Please wear sunscreen and bring enough water for yourself.

Local organizers emphasize their commitment to non-violent action and expect all participants to avoid and de-escalate any confrontation.

For more information: https://www.nokings.org,

Published at the request of local activist Marty McFarland on behalf of Otero County No Kings Protest Committee

item.title: Otero Arts Packs October with Photography, Music, Film and Free Workshops
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Otero Arts has filled its October calendar with a month-long photography exhibit, a baroque chamber concert, an author reading, a lecture on ancient Egypt, a documentary screening and free hands-on workshops, nearly all of them at the Otero Artspace at 12th and Indiana.

The all-volunteer nonprofit, now led by newly elected Board President Kim Melton, opens the month on Thursday, Oct. 1, and keeps something on the schedule almost every week through Oct. 28.

Nature photographer and Otero Arts member Stan Ford headlines the month with a solo show. An opening reception runs Friday, Oct. 2, from 5 to 7 p.m. After that, the exhibit is free and open Thursday through Sunday, 1 to 4 p.m., until it closes Oct. 24.

Ford spent this past May as artist-in-residence at Valles Caldera National Preserve, the third time the National Park Service has chosen him to teach photography at one of its parks. His workshops usually focus on night photography, and this year's class caught a rare sight. Ford said the class was fortunate to see the Northern Lights. Images from the park, including a cabin at sunrise and the aurora over the caldera, are part of the show.

Ford will be at the Artspace on Friday, Oct. 9, from 1 to 4 p.m. to meet members and fellow photographers.

The monthly Free Art Workshop on Saturday, Oct. 10, teaches Imani paper pumpkins with instructor Pennie Espiritu. Reserve a spot by emailing mariaaragon64@gmail.com or signing up at oteroarts.org. The workshop is funded by Thrive! of Southern New Mexico. Espiritu will also preview the craft at the Oct. 1 Meet and Greet.

For more serious painters, Anita Louise West leads a three-day Plein Air Painting Workshop Oct. 13–15, painting historic villages and local landscapes. The cost is $200, and the class is limited to 10 students. A few spaces remain; tickets are at oteroarts.org, and questions go to oteroartsinc@gmail.com.

Reading Series, Friday, Oct. 16, 6 p.m. Jennifer Givhan, a Mexican-American and Indigenous poet and novelist from the Desert Southwest, reads at the Artspace. Givhan has received fellowships from the NEA and PEN/Rosenthal Emerging Voices and won the Southwest Book Award. She has written seven poetry collections and five novels, most recently The Sleeping Sisters.

Cruzando Fronteras, Saturday, Oct. 17, 7 p.m. The Baroque Chamber Ensemble performs music of Bach, Vivaldi, Handel and Scarlatti. Players include Stephen Redfield and Carla Moore on baroque violins, Katie Rietman on baroque cello, Charlotte Mattax Moersch on harpsichord and Gerard Gibbs on recorder. Tickets are $25 at oteroarts.org.

JRI Lecture, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 6 p.m. In the monthly partnership with the Jornada Research Institute, Dave Greenwald presents "Historic Cairo and Ancient Nile Explorations." He previews the sites his tour group will visit this fall, including the Great Pyramids, the inside of the Pyramid of Khufu, the Sphinx and the wider Giza Necropolis.

Film Series, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 5:30 p.m. The documentary The Curious World of Hieronymus Bosch gathers the medieval painter's masterpieces from around the world in his Dutch hometown. Admission is free; donations are welcome.

The month starts with the First Thursdays Meet and Greet on Oct. 1, 10 to 11:30 a.m., with coffee, conversation and Espiritu's paper pumpkin demo. Belly dance classes begin Thursday, Oct. 8, at 5:30 p.m. and continue weekly; contact Claudia Powell at claudia@tularosa.net. The Otero Arts board meets Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 1:30 p.m., and members are welcome.

Elsewhere in the area, Alamogordo MainStreet hosts "Heroes on Mainstreet" Oct. 2, 4 to 8 p.m., on the 900 block of New York Avenue

The Flickinger Center screens the Banff Mountain Film Festival Oct. 9 and stages the Children's Music Theater's "Frozen" Oct. 16–18 and 23–24.

Thrive in Southern New Mexico, an Otero Arts grant provider, holds its Corks & Shells Wine & Pistachio Festival Oct. 17 at Alameda Park. 

The Cloudcroft Art Society's Holiday Show opens Oct. 3, 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

The Otero Artspace is at 1118 Indiana Ave. in Alamogordo. For details, visit oteroarts.org, call 575-446-3880 or email oteroartsinc@gmail.com.

item.title: Stan Ford, Nature Photographer Showing at the Otero Artspace Thursday thru Sunday’s in October
item.description:
Stan Ford, Nature Photographer Showing at the Otero Artspace 

 Otero Arts welcomes back Stan Ford, nature photographer, for a solo show in October.  The exhibit continues through October and closes on Saturday the 24th at 4pm. Free exhibition hours are Thursday thru Sunday 1 pm to 4 pm. 

This past May, Ford was the artist-in-residence at the Valles Caldera National Park. Ford said, “That was a thrill and a bucket list experience for me.” 

 This was the third time he has been selected by the National Park Service to teach photography at one of their parks. “We teach the basics of night/astro-photography and shoot at different locations in the preserve like Longmire’s Cabin (from the TV series “Longmire”) and The “Missing” Cabin (from Ron Howard’s film starring Tommy Lee Jones and Cate Blanchet).”Most of the workshops have been centered upon night photography. 

The classes are free and there is always a lengthy waitlist. This year the class was fortunate to see the Northern Lights,” said Ford.

item.title: Commentary: Same Pattern, Same Silence: Potential Sexual Harassment at Alamogordo City Hall Demands Answers
item.description:
Alamogordo NM Commentary- Over the past 60 days, several city employees have come to us with the same concern: City Hall has become a workplace where comments about appearance are tolerated, assignments seem to follow favor rather than merit, and people are afraid to speak up. These are not new problems here. That is exactly why they deserve answers now.

I am not writing to accuse any individual of a crime. I am writing because what employees describe, if accurate, falls short of the city's own policies and could expose taxpayers to real legal liability.

A double standard on workplace conduct

Employees describe a senior official who has publicly criticized others for using familiar, family-style terms with coworkers, while themself commenting openly on an employee's looks and body. In one instance, employees say the department leader joked that “he should pose for a calendar and could fill all twelve months.” “He could be my Santa January thru December.” 

Swap the genders and few would hesitate to call that inappropriate. Comments about a subordinate's physical appearance are exactly what the city's harassment training warns against. When they come from leadership, they set the tone for everyone below. They also tell employees which rules are enforced, and for whom.

What innuendo costs a workplace

A "joke" about a coworker's body is never only a joke. The EEOC's bipartisan Select Task Force on harassment found that harassment affects all workers, not just the target, and that its true cost includes lost productivity, higher turnover, and reputational harm. The task force's co-chairs testified that lost productivity often shows up as quiet disengagement, and that a bad reputation drives away potential new hires.

The task force also found that harassment too often goes unreported, because people fear being disbelieved, blamed, or punished. In a city government where everyone knows everyone, that fear is magnified. When leaders make suggestive comments in front of staff, every employee learns that appearance is being noticed and graded. Those who object learn to stay quiet, and the best of them start looking for other jobs.

The perception of favoritism

Employees also describe projects being pulled from one manager and handed to another, the same one singled out for comments on his appearance, with no clear explanation. Some department directors are reportedly seen frequently with the city manager outside work, and staff say those directors appear to receive preferential treatment.

Perception matters in public service. Even if every decision has a sound reason, employees who cannot see that reason will fill the gap themselves. That erodes trust, morale, and the city's ability to keep good people.

Meanwhile, some targeted employees have been placed on paid administrative leave. Coworkers worry the pattern targets people who "don't fit the image" leadership wants. Paid leave costs taxpayers twice: once for the person on leave, and again for the work left undone. The public deserves to know the criteria being used.

We have been here before

In 2023, the city added sexual harassment content to commission training after a departing employee raised concerns in an exit interview. Her concern, as it was relayed, was whether appearance affected how some commissioners treated staff.

That same year, the city hired outside counsel to independently investigate the conduct of its commissioners. One sitting commissioner was named in that investigation and again in a second outside investigation in 2025. The December 2023 report found credible evidence that commissioners broke the city's Code of Conduct by going around the city manager to pressure employees.

The same report recorded a former city attorney's exit-interview allegation that a commissioner had engaged in sexual harassment. It found the Code of Conduct gave no clear guidance on handling that complaint, and nothing indicates the allegation was ever investigated. Excerpts of both reports became public only this month, after persistent records requests by Alamogordo Town News. 

Each episode was handled quietly and then forgotten. Employees now see a familiar pattern taking shape, and they have little faith it will be handled differently.

This city has watched leadership scandals play out before, with residents left to absorb the cost.

What this has already cost taxpayers

Alamogordo's habit of settling quietly is well documented:

• About a decade ago, the city agreed to pay $137,500 to its former personnel manager. She alleged she was demoted and fired after supporting a coworker she believed was being treated unfairly.

That coworker, a former public safety lieutenant, settled separately for $250,000.

• In 2023, the city manager left under a retirement and settlement agreement after accusing commissioners of interfering with staff. The outside investigator found his core allegations credible.

• In 2025, a second outside report found the search for a permanent city manager had been "tainted." It warned that passing over the top-scoring candidate, the only woman in the pool, could support a discrimination claim.

• In April 2026, after closed sessions, the commission voted 4–3 to accept a settlement tied to that candidate's EEOC complaint. The terms were not disclosed in open session.

The two figures made public total $387,500 in net pay closer to a half million in total. The rest remain undisclosed, along with the cost of repeated recruitments and outside legal work.

Title VII applies at City Hall

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 covers employers with 15 or more employees, and that includes city governments. Under it, sexual harassment is a form of illegal sex discrimination. It covers unwelcome verbal conduct of a sexual nature that creates an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment, or that interferes with someone's work.

Three points matter here. The person harassed does not have to be the opposite sex of the harasser, so comments by a woman about a man count the same. No one has to be fired or demoted for harassment to be unlawful. And it is separately illegal to retaliate against anyone who complains or cooperates with an investigation.

When a city loses or settles these claims, the bill does not go to the officials involved. It goes to the city's budget and its insurance pool, which means it goes to residents. New Mexico's Human Rights Act adds state-level exposure on top of the federal law.

What the city should do now

The commission can get ahead of this before the next complaint becomes the next settlement:

• Commission an independent review of the current workplace complaints, conducted by an outside HR firm or attorney who reports to the full commission, not the city manager.

• Release the findings of both outside investigation reports in full, with only legally required redactions, and explain what was done about the harassment allegation.

• Disclose the total amount paid in employee settlements over the past ten years.

• Publish the criteria used to place employees on paid administrative leave, and report how many are on leave today and at what cost.

• Require refresher harassment training for all elected officials and senior staff, with attendance made public.

Alamogordo is better than this

This city runs on people who show up: the crews who keep the water running, the clerks who answer every call, the officers and firefighters who work every holiday. They deserve leaders who treat them as professionals, not as gossip or as pin-ups. Most of our elected officials and directors know that, and many have said so on the record.

But respect does not enforce itself. Our charter leaves commissioners to police one another, and the record shows how rarely that happens, how ineffective and how it further supports the good ole boy narrative. Accountability will come only if residents ask for it, out loud and in person.

The next regular commission meeting is Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:30 p.m. Come to public comment. Ask for the reports, the settlement totals, and an independent review. Employees should not have to choose between their careers and a respectful workplace, and residents should not keep learning the truth only after the check clears.

Sources

item.title: Las Cruces sweeps Alamogordo in district soccer
item.description:
Las Cruces NM- Las Cruces scored four times before halftime and beat the Alamogordo boys soccer team 5-1 on Thursday night, keeping the Tigers winless in district play.

Alamogordo, on the road, fell behind in the fourth minute and never recovered. Las Cruces added goals in the 13th and 27th minutes, then a fourth before the break for a 4-0 halftime lead. A fifth came in the 43rd minute, early in the second half.

The Tigers broke through in the 70th minute, when Kyle Tamayo scored off an assist from Ari Cortez. Goalkeeper Noah Mirabal finished with seven saves.

The loss drops Alamogordo to 4-9-2 overall and 0-4 in district. It was the Tigers' second district defeat of the week, following a 6-0 loss to Mayfield.

The Alamogordo girls also fell to Las Cruces on Thursday, losing 3-0. The Lady Tigers are now 3-11-1 overall and 0-4 in district.

Mescalero Apache took a set from Tucumcari but lost in four, 25-14, 25-16, 23-25, 25-14. The Lady Chiefs are 2-11.

Santa Teresa swept Tularosa 25-13, 25-12, 25-20. The Lady Cats are 3-9.

item.title: Alamogordo High School Tigers Homecoming 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Alamogordo High School closes Homecoming Week Friday with a bayou-themed parade down Cuba Avenue and a 5A District 2 football game against the Mayfield Trojans under the lights at Tiger Stadium.

The theme is “A Night on the Bayou.” The parade steps off at 3 p.m. from Alamogordo High School, travels north on Cuba Avenue, then west on 10th Street to Maryland Avenue. Student floats, the band, cheer squads, and community entries are expected along the route. Drivers should plan for temporary slowdowns on Cuba, 10th, and Maryland through the afternoon.

Kickoff is at 7 p.m. at Tiger Stadium, 103 Cuba Ave. The Tigers (2-4, 1-2 in district) host Mayfield (2-4) in a district matchup both teams need. Alamogordo’s last outing was a 54-19 home loss to Artesia on Sept. 25. Mayfield arrives off a 38-22 win over Deming on Sept. 25. Head coach AJ Cisco’s Tigers opened the season with a 41-33 win over Santa Fe and a 28-27 road win at Goddard, and have dropped games to Clovis, Organ Mountain, Roswell, and Artesia.

District materials have framed the week under the slogan “Return the Roar,” with Alamogordo Public Schools asking residents and businesses to stay in black and gold through Saturday, Oct. 3. Homecoming Week began Sept. 28. Wednesday’s powderpuff games raised money for the junior and senior classes. Individual game tickets are sold on the APS website and through the Hometown Tickets app. Season passes covering sports at all levels remain available. Questions go to the APS Call Center at 575-812-8573.

Saturday brings a junior-varsity football home date, another chance for families already in town for the parade and varsity game.

For more than seven decades, Alamogordo’s homecoming has been as much a reunion as a football game: alumni on the sidewalks, storefronts in school colors, and a Friday night that still draws the town to Tiger Stadium. Friday’s doubleheader of parade and kickoff is the center of that week.

Parade and game graphics were released by Alamogordo High School and Alamogordo Public Schools.

item.title: Golden Cube Turns 50: Space Museum to induct Kelly Twins, Mercury 13, and Other Pioneers Saturday Night in Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The New Mexico Museum of Space History marks a half-century on the hill above Alamogordo Saturday night, pairing its Golden Jubilee with the induction of a new class into the International Space Hall of Fame.

The gala, titled “Golden Jubilee: 50 Years of Honoring Yesterday and Inspiring Tomorrow,” runs from 5 to 9 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 3, at the Tays Special Event Center. The museum’s formal dedication was Oct. 5, 1976. Organizers moved the public celebration to the weekend.

Tickets are $90 per person, or $81 for museum members. Dress is semi-formal or business formal. The evening includes a cocktail hour, dinner, a keynote, the induction ceremony, and a silent auction. Doors open at 5 p.m., guests are seated at 6, the program starts at 6:15, the keynote is introduced at 6:30, inductions begin at 7, closing remarks are at 8, and the silent auction is announced at 8:30.

The Class of 2026

The International Space Hall of Fame Foundation Induction Committee selected the class from 45 nominees submitted from around the country. The Governor’s Commission to the New Mexico Museum of Space History confirmed the selections on Feb. 27. The Hall of Fame currently lists 174 inductees, including one team.

The 2026 honorees are:

• The Mercury 13, the 13 American women who, in a privately funded program from 1959 to 1960, completed the same medical and psychological screening used on NASA’s Mercury astronaut candidates. The museum lists them as Jerrie Cobb, Myrtle Cagle, Jane Hart, Rhea Hurrle (Woltman), Jean Hixson, Irene Leverton, Sarah Gorelick (Ratley), Jerri Sloan (Truhill), Bernice Steadman, Gene Nora Stumbough (Jessen), Wally Funk, Jan Dietrich, and Marion Dietrich. Space author Loretta Hall will accept on their behalf.

• Mark Kelly and Scott Kelly, NASA’s identical-twin astronauts. Scott Kelly’s nearly year-long stay on the International Space Station, paired with Mark Kelly as the Earth-bound control, produced the NASA Twins Study on how long-duration flight changes the human body. Mark Kelly is also a U.S. senator from Arizona.

• Michel Mayor, the Swiss astrophysicist who shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics for the first confirmed exoplanet orbiting a sun-like star.

• Creola Katherine Johnson, the NASA mathematician whose trajectory calculations supported Project Mercury, the Apollo missions, and early Space Shuttle flights. Mayor Sharon McDonald will be receiving on the family’s behalf. 

• Dolores “Dee” O’Hara, NASA’s first aerospace nurse, assigned to the Mercury astronauts and a pioneer in space medicine. O’Hara, who recently turned 91, is a confirmed attendee.

“It is an honor and a privilege to welcome the Selectees to Alamogordo for the Induction Ceremony,” Museum Executive Director Karen Kincaid Brady said in the museum’s announcement. In an earlier statement on the class, she tied the evening to both the museum’s 50th year and the nation’s 250th, calling the inductees people “who have dedicated their lives to exploring and understanding our universe.”

A hall of fame born from a baseball commercial

The museum began as an idea in 1973. Former Alamogordo Mayor Dwight Ohlinger, after seeing a commercial for the National Baseball Hall of Fame, argued that if Cooperstown could honor baseball, Alamogordo could honor space — and that the Tularosa Basin, with its rocket and missile history, was the place to do it. Gov. Bruce King folded the proposal into the state’s cultural affairs office. Architects Charles E. Nolan and Associates designed the gold-tinted glass cube. It was dedicated Oct. 5, 1976, as the International Space Hall of Fame and opened to the public on Nov. 23, 1976.

The campus is a Smithsonian Affiliate and a division of the New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs, overseen by the Governor’s Commission. It includes the museum, the Hall of Fame, the John P. Stapp Air and Space Park, the Daisy Track, the Clyde W. Tombaugh Education Center, the New Horizons Dome Theater and Planetarium, and the Astronaut Memorial Garden. On Aug. 8 the museum opened “To Build a Space Museum,” an exhibit on how the golden cube came to be.

Sponsors of Saturday’s gala include the International Space Hall of Fame Foundation, the Sacramento Mountains Foundation, the Buller Family, Future Real Estate, Christus Health, and SkyView2U.

Tickets are available at nmspacemuseum.org and spacehalloffame.org.

item.title: In Memory of James Philip Ottaviano
item.description:
James Philip Ottaviano, 86, of Tularosa, NM, passed at his home on September 22, 2026, surrounded by his wife of 64 years.

Jim was born in Easton, PA and graduated from Easton High School in 1958 before deciding to join the military. In 1958, he enlisted in the U.S. Air Force and spent 4 years serving our country. His last duty station was in Las Vegas, NV where he was set up on a blind date with Julia Benavidez. About 8 months later, Jim would marry Julia in Las Vegas at a chapel on Nellis Air Force Base, end his military service, and move back to his hometown in Pennsylvania to start a family. In Easton they had three daughters, Donna, Judy, and Denise. Jim found work at Mack Printing and IKG steel mill.

In 1979, the family moved to Tularosa, NM, Julia’s hometown. Jim retired from the City of Alamogordo in 2003 after working in the Water, Parks and Recreation, and Street departments.

Jim had a love for singing and playing guitar. In his 20s, he joined a singing quartet called The Flashers. Jim taught himself how to play guitar and enjoyed performing for friends and family on his Gibson electric guitar and a 12-string. He taught his nephew Sammy Joe Vigil how to play guitar who became a talented musician. He also played trumpet and played Reveille, Retreat and Taps while in the Air Force.

Jim was an excellent cook, being the “head chef” for the family his whole life. Everything he cooked was delicious from steak and chicken, to pizza and pasta. No one will ever forget the many times he would camp with the family and make spaghetti and meatballs for everyone.

Jim will probably best be known for his sense of humor and joking around. Until the very end, he was cracking jokes and making us laugh. Many will probably remember his pranks, telling funny stories, and ability to make people laugh.

Jim is preceded in death by his parents, Anthony and Josephine Ottaviano. He is survived by his wife Julia, of 64 years; his daughters, Donna Ottaviano (Chris) of Las Cruces, NM, Denise Ottaviano and Judy Ottaviano of Tularosa, NM; his granddaughters, Sarah Dysinger and Alicia Ruiz (Tom); great grandchildren, TJ, Eva, Andrew, and Zoey Ruiz. He is also survived by his brother, Charles Ottaviano (Marilyn); sisters, Annamarie Thatcher (Ron) and Beatrice Ann Wagner (Jeff).

The family extends its deepest gratitude to Jim's hospice nurse, Erva, who cared for him with such love and compassion, and provided the family with much needed comfort and support.

Cremation has taken place. The eulogy and visitation will be held at St. Francis De Paula Catholic Church in Tularosa, NM on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at 9:30 am followed by a mass at 10:00 am. Burial will follow at Sacred Heart Cemetery in Tularosa. Lunch will be served at a celebration of life at the Ottaviano home following burial.

item.title: Child abuse arrests, domestic violence and DWIs fill Alamogordo police log for Sept. 21–27
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Three child abuse arrests, eight domestic violence cases and five DWI arrests were among the incidents Alamogordo police logged between Sept. 21 and Sept. 27, 2026.

The department's weekly activity log lists 59 arrests, citations and juvenile referrals for the week, plus one recovered stolen vehicle. Most of those arrested were booked into the Otero County Detention Center (OCDC) pending court appearances.

The log covers major activity only and does not include every call for service. Everyone listed is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

Three adults were arrested on child abuse charges, and all three were booked into OCDC.

Two men were arrested on aggravated assault charges after separate disturbances on Sept. 21. One was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, the other with two counts of aggravated assault.

Eight cases involved offenses against household members:

In other cases, a man was arrested Sept. 22 for assault on a peace officer, criminal trespass, disorderly conduct and impersonating a peace officer. A man was cited Sept. 27 for battery and criminal damage to property after a disturbance.

Seven people faced drug charges, three of them arrested with the White Mountain Drug Task Force.

Three others were charged with possession of drug paraphernalia alongside other offenses: a trespassing arrest on Sept. 21, a warrant arrest on Sept. 22 and a citation on Sept. 24.

Officers made five DWI arrests during the week.

Four 17-year-olds were referred to juvenile probation for alcohol offenses. Two boys were referred Sept. 24 from the same disturbance that led to a DWI arrest and a resisting arrest.

A third boy was referred in a case that also brought drinking-in-public citations for two men on Sept. 25. A girl located after a runaway report on Sept. 27 was referred and released to a parent.

Officers recovered a stolen vehicle Sept. 24 in the 1500 block of Hawaii Avenue and returned it to its owner. Two people were contacted during stolen vehicle investigations that day: one was arrested on an unrelated warrant, the other cited for drug paraphernalia and traffic violations. The log lists no vehicle theft charge for either and says the investigation continues.

Six cases involved trespassing, including three arrests on Sept. 21 alone.

Thirteen entries were warrants for missed court dates, unpaid fines or release violations, the largest single category of the week.

Two traffic stops led to arrests beyond the DWI cases. A man was arrested Sept. 23 for concealing identity and driving on a suspended or revoked license. A man was arrested Sept. 25 for driving while revoked, reckless driving, no insurance, a registration violation and resisting an officer.

The full weekly log, including case numbers, is posted by the City of Alamogordo: September 21 to September 27, 2026 (PDF).

Reports on individual incidents can be requested at www.alamogordopd.com under "Request a Report," or from the police Records Division at 575-439-4300.

item.title: Factcheck: Block Mailer Claims Credit for Money Every House Member Got — Including Bills He Opposed and Bills That Died
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — A campaign postcard from Rep. John Block tells District 51 he “delivered more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County priorities and passed legislation to expand funding for critical water projects and infrastructure.” The Legislative Council Service’s own sponsor chart, and the House roll calls, do not say that.

The 2026 funded-projects report lists seven projects under Block’s name, totaling $2,500,000. The same report lists $2,500,000 for Rep. Gail Armstrong and $2,500,000 for Rep. Brian Baca. An Appropriations and Finance Committee handout from July 2025 says the 2025 session allocated $2.5 million to every representative and $4.2 million to every senator. The figure on the card is not the figure on the chart.

His 2026 list is Alamogordo High School facility work, $650,000; Alamogordo municipal facility improvements, $300,000; Alamogordo police vehicles, $100,000; New Mexico Museum of Space History improvements, $730,436; a New Mexico National Guard museum project in Santa Fe County, $20,000; an Otero County dispatch facility, $326,564; and an Otero County dump truck, $373,000. One of the seven is not in the district. A 2024 request form asked for far more, including $3 million for a Mescalero fire substation. A request is not an appropriation.

Capital outlay in New Mexico is not a bill a rank-and-file member sponsors and passes. About half the capital bill is statewide. The other half is split among the House, the Senate and the governor. The House half is divided evenly. Each member turns in a list. Those lists are folded into one bill and the bill passes or fails as a package.

Block voted no on that package. Block is misleading constituents on the process and his own actions. 

On the 2025 capital-outlay bill, House Bill 450, the House roll call records him as No. The bill passed and was signed April 11, 2025. His projects were in the bill he voted against. On the 2025 General Appropriation Act, House Bill 2, Vote Smart records him as No. The House vote was 50-18. He was one of the 18 no votes voting against the very appropriate he claims credit for delivering. The bill was signed as Chapter 160.

That is the dishonesty in the $11 million line by NM State Representative John Block’s. He did not sponsor the appropriation. He submitted a list, as every member does. He voted against the bill that approved the list

The bill passed without him!

A member who wants credit for the projects votes for the bill, or he tells voters the projects passed over his objection. He does not get both!

If “more than $11 million” is a multi-year sum of equal shares, it is still the automatic allocation, not a sum he won. Four sessions at $2.5 million is $10 million, and only if every year’s share was that large. The postcard does not show that math. Figures from 2022 belong to his predecessor.

The water line has the same problem of degree

House Bill 63 of 2026 is a real law, and his name is on it, second. The introduced text reads “Kathleen Cates and John Block and Pete Campos.” The fiscal impact report lists the sponsor as Cates/Block. It passed unanimously and was signed as Chapter 35. Eileen Acres and the Mescalero Apache Tribe are on a statewide list of 75 entities. He did not pass it. He was the second name on a committee-endorsed authorization.

The cost line does not survive his own bills.

The card says he fought bills that would raise gas and energy costs and sponsored legislation to lower taxes on small businesses.

Fact: House Bill 45 of 2025, which he introduced, was a 3.75 percent excise tax on wind, solar and geothermal generation. It would have raised your PNM bill and energy costs It died. 

On House Bill 91, the low-income utility rate structure, he voted no.

The small-business gross-receipts bills he sponsored or co-sponsored, including a 2023 deduction, died in committee

Pressing PNM at a public hearing is not a statute it’s theatre! 

The veterans line uses “sponsored and passed” for measures that were not his and did not pass. 

The card says he passed a bill to make moving to New Mexico easier for military families, expanded property-tax relief for veterans, and sponsored a measure to let veterans keep 100 percent of retirement pay. A move-in bill framed that way is not on his sponsor list. The property-tax piece was a 2023 joint resolution he co-sponsored. The exemption voters adopted was carried by other members. The 100 percent retirement exemption, House Bill 221 of 2026, died in committee. The cap is still $30,000.

Set next to the sponsorship record, the mailer is one argument told twice. He led no bill into law in 2025 or 2026.

The crime bill voters may have heard about was Representative Reeb’s. The water bill was Cates’s. The money on the card is the House share, and he voted no on the 2025 bills that contained it.

Ineffective is the committee docket. Dishonest is the postcard’s decision to describe that docket, and that no vote, as delivery.

Check the facts for yourself!

Note:  John Block is in a competitive election that the Santa Fe New Mexican called “the race of his life” running against lifelong Alamogordo resident and Independent, Grace Nagamine. Nagamine’s platform focused on local issues can be found at 
https://graceforhd51.org/

John Block; Bill Sponsor roll call, House Bill 450 (2025), Block no, signed April 11, 2025; Vote Smart, House Bill 2 (2025) House final passage, John Block, District 51, no; LegiScan, House Bill 2 (2025), House 50-18, Chapter 160; nmlegis.gov, House Bill 63 (2026) introduced text; Legislative Finance Committee fiscal impact report on House Bill 63, Jan. 26, 2026; BillTrack50, House Bill 63, Chapter 35, March 5, 2026; governor’s Executive Message No. 18, House Bill 36, April 11, 2025.

item.title: Class of 1986 Returns for Homecoming; Gathering to Honor Coach Marilyn Sepulveda
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Members of the Alamogordo High School Class of 1986 are back in town this homecoming weekend for their 40-year reunion.

Classmates have a full slate of activities planned, with plenty of reminders of their days as Tigers. For many, the weekend is a chance to trade old stories and reconnect with friends they have not seen in decades.

One event reaches well beyond a single graduating class. Alumni from the Class of 1986, other classes and other former athletes will meet at noon at the 19th Hole restaurant and bar to celebrate the life and accomplishments of Marilyn Sepulveda. The award-winning cross country and track and field coach mentored many of them.

The celebration and remembrance is open to the public. Former students, former athletes and anyone who knew Sepulveda are invited to attend.

Sepulveda died of cancer in 1989, three years after the Class of 1986 graduated. In 2025, the New Mexico High School Coaches Association inducted her posthumously into its Hall of Honor.

Born Marilyn McDonald on Jan. 28, 1945, in Telluride, Colorado, Sepulveda began her career in Alamogordo in 1965. She started as a physical education instructor, then moved into English and coaching.

She became the first woman in New Mexico to coach both boys' and girls' cross country, while also leading the girls' track and field program. That team won its first district title in 1975, a year after it was formed, and finished second at state.

Under Sepulveda, the girls' track and field program won 14 district championships and one state title. It also earned four state runner-up trophies and two third-place finishes. Her 1982 cross country team placed third at the state championships.

The honors followed. In 1981, she became the first Alamogordo coach named Girls Track and Field Coach of the Year by the New Mexico High School Coaches Association. She also earned the association's Level IV Coaching Milestone ring.

On July 31, 1987, she led a group of coaches in founding the New Mexico Track and Cross Country Coaches Association. She served as its first president until her death and remains on its Presidents Wall of Fame. That same year, she was appointed vice chair for Region 8 of the National High School Coaches Association.

Coaching ran in the family. Her husband, Bob Sepulveda will be present at the event, won five state championships as Alamogordo's boys track and field coach, and both are on the Alamogordo Tiger Wall of Fame. Their son, Rene Sepulveda, spent nearly two decades coaching in the NCAA Big 12 Conference sending multiple athletes to Olympic training and winning national awards. He will also be onsite to discuss his mother’s history and impact on generations of students.

item.title: Bowman's three touchdowns carry Alamogordo past Mayfield, 24-19
item.description:
Alamogordo N. M- What a way to celebrate homecoming.

One week after a 54-19 loss to Artesia, Alamogordo gave its homecoming crowd plenty to cheer about Friday night. Tristan Bowman rushed for three touchdowns, and the Tigers beat Mayfield 24-19 on their home field.

It was the turnaround this team needed. Alamogordo had lost four of its previous five games and dropped its last two at home by a combined 110-45. On Friday, the Tigers held an opponent under 20 points for the first time all season.

Bowman was the star of the night. He found the end zone from 2, 18 and 8 yards out and added a two-point conversion run, accounting for 20 of his team's 24 points. Kicker Gabe Russell supplied the other four with a 35-yard field goal and an extra point.

Alamogordo trailed only once, 5-3 in the second quarter. The Tigers answered with 21 straight points and led 24-5 after three quarters.

Mayfield made it interesting. Levi Montez ran for one touchdown and threw for another in the fourth quarter, cutting the margin to five with 4:53 left. The Tigers shut the door from there, and the homecoming celebration was on.

The victory lifts Alamogordo to 3-4 overall and 2-2 in district play. It is the Tigers' first home win since the Aug. 21 season opener against Santa Fe.

How the scoring went

First quarter. Russell put Alamogordo on the board with a 35-yard field goal with 3:15 left. Mayfield got two points back on a safety, and the Tigers led 3-2 at the end of the quarter.

Second quarter. Ryan Chavez kicked a 28-yard field goal with 7:18 left to give Mayfield a 5-3 lead. Bowman answered with a 2-yard touchdown run with 4:59 left and ran in the two-point conversion himself. Alamogordo led 11-5 at halftime.

Third quarter. Bowman scored on an 18-yard run with 8:49 left, and Russell's extra point made it 18-5. Bowman added an 8-yard touchdown run with 3:28 left. The extra point missed, leaving the score 24-5 after three quarters.

Fourth quarter. Montez scored on a 7-yard run with 9:02 left, and the extra point cut the lead to 24-12. He then threw a 19-yard touchdown pass with 4:53 left, and the kick made it 24-19. Neither team scored again.

Momentum heading into Gadsden

The Tigers now have a win to build on. Alamogordo sits fourth in 5A District 2 and travels to Gadsden on Oct. 16 with a chance to even its record at 4-4.

Homecoming weekend has more to celebrate than one win. In other Tiger sports news, the Class of 1986 and former athletes gather at noon Saturday at the 19th Hole to honor the late Coach Marilyn Sepulveda, a pioneer of girls' athletics in New Mexico. Read more: Class of 1986 Returns for Homecoming; Gathering to Honor Coach Marilyn Sepulveda.

From the legends who built Tiger athletics to the players carrying it forward, it is a good weekend to be a Tiger. The Tiger class of 86 reunion gala will also be tonight - roaring through the city with Tiger pride this homecoming weekend.

item.title: Early Voting Begins Oct 6, in Alamogordo- What to Know.
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Early voting for the Nov. 3 general election opens Tuesday, Oct. 6, at the Otero County Administration Building, the only Alamogordo site open that first week. Expanded early voting begins Saturday, Oct. 17, and early voting ends Saturday, Oct. 31. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Voters do not have to give a reason to vote early. Absentee ballots also begin going out Oct. 6 to people who have already applied. The last day to request a mail ballot is Tuesday, Oct. 20. Voted absentee ballots must be received by 7 p.m. on Election Day.

Where to vote early in Alamogordo

• Otero County Administration Building, 1101 N. New York Ave., Room 101. Oct. 6 through Oct. 31, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. This is the county’s in-person absentee and early-voting office for the opening stretch.

• Otero County Fairgrounds, 401 Fairgrounds Road. Oct. 17 through Oct. 31, Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., according to the city listing.

• In-person absentee marking at the Otero County Clerk’s Office, 1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite C, Oct. 19 through Oct. 30, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Statewide, expanded early voting at alternate sites begins Oct. 17 and ends Oct. 31. Voters should confirm the latest hours before they go, especially around Indigenous Peoples’ Day, Monday, Oct. 12, when many clerk offices are closed.

The clerk’s office can be reached at 575-437-4942. Registration, a sample ballot, and an absentee application are at nmvote.org. Same-day registration is available at early-voting sites and on Election Day for eligible voters.

Election Day in the city

On Nov. 3, any Otero County voter may use a voting convenience center.

City sites posted by Alamogordo are the Fairgrounds, the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center at 800 E. First St., and the Tays Special Events Center at 2400 N. Scenic Drive, all open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Who is on the ballot

This is a midterm general election, not a city commission election. Alamogordo’s commission races were decided in the 2025 regular local election. The November ballot is federal, statewide, legislative, county, judicial, and bond questions. A voter’s exact ballot depends on address. The official sample ballot is at nmvote.org and on the Otero County Clerk’s “2026 General Election Super Sample Ballot.”

At the top of the ballot:

• U.S. Senate: Democrat Ben Ray Luján and Republican Larry Marker.

• U.S. House, District 2 (covers Otero County): Democrat Gabe Vasquez and Republican Gregory Cunningham.

• Governor: Democrat Deb Haaland, with running mate Stephanie Garcia Richard, and Republican Gregg Hull, with running mate David Gallegos. Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is term-limited.

• Secretary of state: Democrat Amanda López Askin and Republican Ramona Goolsby.

Legislative races that touch Otero County:

• House District 51: Republican incumbent John Block and independent Grace A. Nagamine.

• House District 53: Republican Ben Luna Jr., who did not draw a general-election opponent in the June independent-filing window.

• House District 56: Republican incumbent Harlan Vincent.

• Senate District 33 (parts of Otero, Lincoln, and Chaves counties): Democrat William Griffin and Republican Rex Wilson.

County races filed for November:

• Commission District 1: Republican Christopher Wayne Glidden and Democrat Alan David Gonzalez.

• Commission District 2: Republican Jonathan T. Emery and independent Evan Christopher Lambert.

• Sheriff: Republican Geraldine Yazza Martinez, who won a three-way June primary and is uncontested.

• Assessor: Republican James M. Bowman, unopposed.

• Probate judge: Jessica Lynn Suggs, listed as unopposed.

Judicial questions include retention of 12th Judicial District judges, including Stephen P. Ochoa and Angie K. Schneider, a special election for Division 2, and magistrate races. Retention is a yes-or-no vote, not a contest between candidates.

Statewide questions include four constitutional amendments and three general-obligation bonds. The amendments cover the governor’s pocket veto, school-election timing, a salary for legislators tied to median household income, and university regent appointments. The bonds are for senior facilities (about $21.6 million), libraries (about $19.3 million), and higher-education, special-school, and tribal-school projects (about $352.2 million), repaid with a statewide property-tax levy. Otero County also has a local bond question on the ballot.

What to bring

New Mexico does not require photo identification for most voters. First-time voters who registered by mail and did not provide ID then may be asked for identification. Anyone unsure of status, precinct, or ballot should look up the record at nmvote.org or call the clerk before Tuesday.

item.title: IPRA Task Force Issues Recommendations to the Legislature
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — The state task force charged with reviewing New Mexico’s Inspection of Public Records Act has sent lawmakers 11 recommendations, including an out-of-state fee for police body-camera review, a new ombudsman, and factors courts would weigh before imposing the law’s daily penalties. Open-government members on the panel voted against the pieces most likely to change how the public enforces the statute.

The letter went Thursday to the interim Courts, Corrections and Justice Committee and the Legislative Finance Committee. It is not the final report. The task force said that report, with majority and minority positions and the public comments it received, is due by Oct. 15. House Joint Memorial 2, sponsored by Rep. Cathrynn N. Brown and co-sponsored by Sen. Natalie Figueroa and Rep. Matthew McQueen, directed the New Mexico Department of Justice to convene the panel and report on IPRA’s “workability and effectiveness.”

The Santa Fe New Mexican reported Friday that the letter appeared on the Department of Justice website that morning and that references to it were gone by 5:30 p.m. The task-force page still describes the panel and its listening tour, including the June 22 stop in Alamogordo.

The eight-member panel held 11 public meetings — Clovis, Roswell, Carlsbad, Alamogordo, Las Cruces, Silver City, Gallup, Farmington, Las Vegas, Santa Fe, and Albuquerque — and took 312 comments in person and online. It then held seven deliberative meetings. Members are Madeleine Zaritsky of the Department of Justice, who chaired the panel; Rebecca Martinez of the New Mexico Municipal League; Michael Eshleman of the New Mexico Association of Counties, a former Otero County attorney; Belinda Mills of the New Mexico Press Association; Lalita Moskowitz of the ACLU of New Mexico; Kenneth Stalter, a plaintiff’s attorney; Ethan Watson, a defense attorney; and Greg Williams of the New Mexico Foundation for Open Government.

What drew opposition

The sharpest split is on fees, penalties, and a new office that would sit between requestors and court.

Six members favored a statutory scheme requiring out-of-state requestors to pay the actual cost of reviewing and redacting body-camera footage. Any residency rule, the letter says, should account for victims, people who are indigent or unhoused, legitimate newsgathering, and other out-of-state requestors with a real interest in New Mexico records. Fees collected would have to be dedicated to IPRA staffing, technology, training, and redaction. Moskowitz opposed it. Eshleman abstained.

Six members favored an IPRA ombudsman, or similar office, that would train both sides, run a hotline, issue non-binding advisory opinions, mediate, and collect compliance data for the Legislature. Moskowitz and Williams opposed that recommendation. An advisory office that does not bind agencies can become a delay if custodians treat it as a substitute for the deadlines and damages already in the statute.

Five members favored a non-exclusive list of factors for courts deciding statutory per-diem penalties under Section 14-2-11 and whether a denial was unreasonable. Moskowitz and Williams opposed it. Mills abstained. IPRA’s daily penalty is the main consequence when a custodian misses a deadline or withholds a record without a lawful exemption. A factor list written for agencies can narrow that remedy without an explicit repeal.

What passed with less friction

Three recommendations were unanimous: more money to digitize paper records, including large-format building plans; proactive publication of record classes that do not need redaction, plus a public portal for a person’s own traffic-crash report; and a duty for a requestor to answer a custodian’s good-faith fee demand within a set time or have the request closed.

Seven members backed standardized statewide reporting of IPRA data, possibly with a volume threshold. Martinez opposed it. Seven backed more training tied to custodians’ needs and the Department of Justice training budget. Walker Boyd, sitting as Eshleman’s proxy, opposed it. Seven backed a credentialing program in public records, through a state agency or a New Mexico university. Zaritsky abstained. Seven backed grants so public bodies can buy request-management and redaction software. Stalter did not vote.

Seven members also backed a coordinated review of the Children’s Code, victims’ rights statutes, and IPRA confidentiality rules, with attention to whether protections follow a record when it moves to law enforcement, a district attorney, or another public body. The letter says any change should not create exemptions broad enough to block oversight. Moskowitz opposed it.

Why it matters here

Alamogordo Town News has used IPRA and the Open Meetings Act to obtain city and county records on hiring, budgets, ethics complaints, and closed-door commission business. Those requests are in-state newsgathering, not commercial harvesting of body-camera video. The letter’s own caveat for “legitimate newsgathering” is the line the 2027 session will have to write in statute if the body-camera fee moves forward. A fee that local outlets can waive on paper and still cannot pay in practice is a barrier.

The Department of Justice page frames the review around request volume that has more than doubled since 2020, commercial data brokers, and out-of-state and out-of-country filers. Open-government groups on the panel have argued that volume is not a reason to weaken the right of New Mexicans to inspect the records their governments already hold.

The full report, including rejected ideas and the comment appendices, is scheduled for the same two committees by Oct. 15. Nothing in the letter is law. Each item still needs a bill, a hearing, and a vote in the 2027 session.

item.title: Analysis: Nagamine Draws Clear Lines on Data Centers While Block Lets His News Site Speak
item.description:
Summary

Nagamine: a concrete policy stance. A data center proposal must have closed-loop water, a noise mitigation plan and its own power with no effect on the grid or on local residents, or it would not be considered.

Block: no position in his own name was found. The news site he founded and edits has welcomed the state’s largest data center project and criticized those who would pause the industry, which amounts to a tacit endorsement.

 Endorsement: the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter confirmed its endorsement of Nagamine on Aug. 29.

 Caveat: Block’s stance is inferred from what his site publishes, not from a statement or a vote.

ALAMOGORDO — On data centers, the two candidates for House District 51 have given voters very different amounts to go on. Independent Grace Nagamine has laid out specific conditions a project must meet or not be considered. She also carries the endorsement of the Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter into the Nov. 3 election.

State Rep. John Block, R-Alamogordo, has not taken a position in his own name, as far as a search for this article found. The Piñon Post, the conservative news site he founded and edits, has done the talking. It has welcomed the industry’s largest New Mexico project and gone after the politicians who want to slow it.

Nagamine’s stand

Nagamine has said a data center proposal must meet three conditions or it would not be considered:

• A noise mitigation plan

• Self-sustaining power, separate from the grid, with no effect on electric rates for neighboring communities, small businesses or residents

• Closed-loop water use that does not draw on local aquifers or on areas already short of water

The position is conditional, not a ban. It stops short of the statewide moratorium that Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and some Doña Ana County legislators have proposed.

It fits the rest of her campaign. Her published platform calls water the district’s most urgent fight and pledges to pursue state funding for Alamogordo’s water and sewer rebuild.

In a September video reported by Alamogordo Town News, she listed high electric prices among the issues she said the race should be about.

The Sierra Club endorsement

The Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter confirmed its endorsement of Nagamine in an Aug. 29 email from Richard Barish, the chapter’s political chair. The email followed a phone call and said she was free to announce it at any time.

Barish thanked her for “stepping up to run for the legislature” and for her commitment to the district’s residents. He said the chapter would list its endorsements in the October-December issue of its quarterly newsletter.

The chapter’s own position on the issue is public. In a Sept. 17 statement, it said it supports a moratorium on data centers until enforceable guardrails are in place, citing climate pollution, water and electric bills.

Nagamine’s conditions address the same concerns, water and electric rates among them, without calling for a moratorium.

Block and the Piñon Post

The site’s author page identifies Block as its founder and editor. Its data center articles carry a “Piñon Post” staff byline however he is owner and editor responsible for all content decisions. 

A June 23 article on Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI campus in Doña Ana County, said the project could become “a major win for southern New Mexico” if it delivers on its promises. It answered water concerns with Oracle’s figure of about 11 million gallons of non-potable water in closed-loop systems. It acknowledged drought, said New Mexico should grow, and called for transparency and long-term protections trusting the sponsoring company statements without challenge.

Since mid-September the site has focused on Haaland. A Sept. 27 article set her moratorium pledge against at least $117,200 in contributions it tied to Oracle and industry executives. The same article said there is no evidence the money changed her positions.

Searchlight New Mexico reported that Oracle and BorderPlex also gave a little more than $51,000 to Republicans, including $10,000 each to Rep. Nicole Chavez and Sen. Larry Scott.

Block has spoken about the race, if not about data centers. In a fundraising email reported by the Santa Fe New Mexican, he said his opponent is backed by a deep-pocketed, far-left political action committee however she is an Independent and has reported support from both sides of the isle including an endorsement from former Republican Mayor of Alamogordo, Susan Payne. 

How this comparison was made for this article.

The two candidates are measured here on different kinds of evidence, and readers should weigh them differently.

Nagamine’s position comes from her own stated conditions and her published platform.

Block’s comes from what the site he edits has chosen to publish. That is an editorial record on a property he uses to attack his political opponents and is well known as his mouthpiece.

On that evidence, the difference is one of starting point. The Piñon Post owned by John Block begins from growth and treats water and power as questions to settle along the way.

Nagamine would require her conditions to be met before a project is considered.

The two overlap in places. The June article cited on-site fuel cells and closed-loop, non-potable water, features that resemble two of Nagamine’s conditions. It did not address noise or neighbors’ electric rates.

The question is not yet local. Project Jupiter is in Santa Teresa, outside House District 51. Otero County has no approved large data center, though commissioners directed staff in March to explore the idea, Alamogordo Town News reported.

Conclusion

Nagamine has given voters a concrete policy stance. A data center proposal would need closed-loop water, a noise mitigation plan and its own power, with no effect on the grid and no cost to local residents. Without those, it would not be considered.

Block has not matched that in his own name. He has left the question unaddressed while the site he controls presents Project Jupiter as an economic opportunity and aims its criticism at those who would pause the industry. Taken together, that amounts to a tacit endorsement by John Block of data centers, delivered through his publication instead of his office.

That conclusion rests on inference, and Block can settle it. He could say how he would vote on a statewide pause and what conditions, if any, he would require of a data center in Otero County.

Nagamine has lead with a concrete policy stance where is the leadership from John Block?

• Nagamine’s data center conditions: provided to the author; date and venue to be added

item.title: The Minority Excuse: Measuring Rep. John Block Against His Own Caucus
item.description:
Twenty-five of 26 House Republicans had a bill signed into law in 2026. Block’s pass rate ranks 19th of 26, in the bottom 10 of his caucus. He led none of the bills that carry his name into law, and every proposal of his own failed.

ALAMOGORDO N.M. — When Rep. John Block’s thin legislative record comes up, the answer from his defenders is always the same. He is a Republican in a Democratic Legislature. The minority cannot pass bills. Judge him on something else.

So judge him against Republicans. We pulled the 2026 session record of every one of the 26 Republicans in the New Mexico House, the people who sit in the same minority, face the same committee chairs and answer to the same governor. Measured against them (fellow Republicans), Block is in the bottom third in effectiveness.

Block put his name on 37 bills, memorials and resolutions in 2026. Four passed but none that he actually sponsored to begin with. That is a success rate of 10.8%, and it ranks 19th in a caucus of 26. Only seven Republicans did worse. The caucus median is 13.8%. The average is 16.3%.

The members at the top are not household names with safe majorities behind them. Republican Rep. Jack Chatfield passed 42.9% of what he sponsored. Republicans; Rep. William Hall passed 33.3%. Rep. Brian Baca, 31.3%. Rep. Tanya Mirabal Moya, 27.3%. Rep. Catherine Cullen, a first-term member, 20.8%. Minority Leader Gail Armstrong passed seven of 40.

The bottom 10, in order, are Reps. Stefani Lord, Rebecca Dow, John Block, Alan Martinez, Jimmy Mason, Elaine Sena Cortez, Luis Terrazas, Rodney Montoya, Randall Pettigrew and Martin Zamora.

Cut the numbers another way and the picture holds. By the share of his measures that became law, Block is 18th. Among the 21 Republicans who sponsored at least 15 measures, he is 15th. Twenty-five of the 26 had a bill signed by the governor, so the minority can plainly pass legislation. First-term Republican Rep. Nicole Chavez had five.

A bill changes the law. A memorial is a statement of the Legislature’s wishes and changes nothing. A sponsor is anyone who signs on; the first-listed sponsor is the legislator who brought the bill and carried it.

Three bills that became law in 2026 have Block’s name on them. He was the first-listed sponsor on none. The medical malpractice overhaul was led by a Democrat, Rep. Christine Chandler, and by Armstrong; 49 legislators signed it, including 23 of the 26 House Republicans. The police battery bill was Rep. Andrea Reeb’s. The water project bill lists Democratic Rep. Kathleen Cates first and Block second, and came out of an interim committee. His one successful memorial, asking for a film industry task force, was a Democrat’s.

Everything Block brought on his own failed. Thirty-three measures, among them permitless carry of firearms, voter identification, chemical castration as a parole condition, a new tax on renewable energy production and year-round daylight saving time. Several were repeats of bills that failed in 2023. Most never got out of their first committee.

One of his measures passed the full House before dying in the Senate. Chavez had 13 reach that stage. Sena Cortez had nine. Armstrong, Cullen and Rep. Jenifer Jones had eight each. Those are bills that Democratic chairs agreed to hear and Democratic members agreed to vote for. That takes relationships.

Block’s campaign postcard tells voters he “delivered more than $11 million for Alamogordo and Otero County priorities.”

Here is how that money works. Each year the House divides its share of capital outlay evenly. Each member turns in a list of projects, the lists are folded into one bill, and the bill passes or fails as a package. A legislative finance handout put the 2025 share at $2.5 million for every representative. The Legislative Council Service chart for 2026 shows seven projects under Block’s name totaling exactly $2.5 million, the same figure it shows for Armstrong and Baca. The money on the postcard is the standard share, added up over four years.

Then look at how he voted on the packages. In 2023 he voted no on House Bill 505. In 2025 he voted no on House Bill 450, and no on the state budget. In 2026 he voted no on Senate Bill 240 and no on the capital outlay reauthorization bill. He picked the projects, voted against the bills that paid for them, and mailed voters a card taking credit.

In the final week of the 2026 session he was also recorded absent on four bills, including wheelchair insurance coverage and the Child Care Assistance Program Act.

Block came to Santa Fe as the publisher of the Piñon Post, a site that, as the Santa Fe New Mexican has reported, routinely labels Democrats “far-left.” Before he held office he filed a campaign finance complaint against the governor over hair and makeup expenses; the Secretary of State’s Office found no violation. In November 2024 the secretary of state told a legislative committee she had been harassed online, and her office named Block as the member she meant. Block denied it and called the accusation a publicity stunt.

No record can prove that those fights are why his bills die. That is a conclusion after speaking with members of both parties that work along side him. 

But the contrast in the data is hard to miss. The Republicans who passed bills in 2026 attached themselves to work that could win Democratic votes: licensing compacts to bring health care workers into the state, parole and pension fixes, property tax relief for disabled veterans. 

Block spent his session on bills with no path, in a building where the people he has spent years attacking decide what gets a hearing.

Four years in, his record is 174 measures sponsored and 11 signed bills carrying his name. Being in the minority explains why Republican bills are hard to pass. It does not explain why 18 other Republicans passed a larger share of theirs.

District 51 voters have a choice this year, that by Block's Party's own admission has become "a race of a lifetime." Unlike Block, Grace Nagamine is  a lifelong Alamogordo resident running as an independent, and claims to be beholden to the constituents not the party ideology of either party and  is on the Nov. 3 ballot against Block.

Where Block offers a mailer, Nagamine has published detailed position statements and draft legislation at graceforhd51.org, so voters can read what she would file before they vote. Where Block has built a brand on picking fights with the people who run the Capitol, she has committed to building collaborations with members of both parties. As an independent she owes neither caucus a vote.

The case for that approach is in the numbers above. Collaboration is how dollars and support reach rural New Mexico communities.
