item.title: Letter on City Hall Workplace Concerns Reaches Commission, Press and Former City Leaders; City Manager Responds
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — An anonymous letter raising workplace conduct concerns at Alamogordo City Hall has reached the mayor and City Commission, city administration, AlamogordoTownNews and former members of the city’s staff leadership.

The letter repeats concerns that city employees first described to AlamogordoTownNews for our Oct. 1 commentary. City Manager Robert Stockwell confirmed Monday that City Hall received it, and he responded in writing the same evening.

The letter’s author is unknown and its claims have not been verified. AlamogordoTownNews is withholding the names, titles and departments it identifies, along with details that could point to specific employees, given allegations are not proven. 

Who received the letter

The letter is addressed to the mayor, the mayor pro tem, the five city commissioners and Human Resources. Stockwell confirmed City Hall received it Monday and said it “has been distributed to the Mayor and Commissioners.”

AlamogordoTownNews received the same letter by mail, in an envelope postmarked Oct. 3. Copies also went to former members of the city’s staff leadership, AlamogordoTownNews has learned.

That distribution puts the concerns in front of people inside and outside current city government. The writer identifies as a city employee. “I am making this report anonymously because I am afraid of retaliation,” the letter states.

What the letter raises

The one-page letter raises three concerns and asks that each be looked into.

• Perceived favoritism. The writer describes what appears to be a close relationship between senior leaders, including long closed-door meetings. Employees believe it gives one department head outsized access and influence, the letter says, and it is hurting morale. The writer states they have not personally witnessed anything physical or romantic and do not want to claim otherwise.

 A possible conflict of interest. The writer asks whether a relationship between two senior staff members of equal rank could lead to different treatment in city financial decisions. The writer says they were told the relationship does not violate city policy.

Comments about an employee’s appearance. The writer reports, under the city’s sexual harassment policy, hearing a supervisor comment more than once on a subordinate’s physical appearance. The comments were not directed at the  letter writer.

The writer says the report is not meant to cause trouble. The letter cites the city’s stated zero-tolerance policy and asks that the concerns “at least be looked into.”

The city manager responds

Stockwell answered in three emails to AlamogordoTownNews on Monday evening.

He denied any improper conduct on his own part.

“There is no improper relationship between me and any employees of the city,” he wrote. He said he fully understands his role and would not compromise his impartiality and professionalism toward city employees, or the integrity of any employee.

He said private meetings with senior staff are routine.

“I routinely meet with the senior staff behind closed doors dealing with matters that must be kept confidential and/or often to simply block out conversations and noise from hallways and adjoining offices.”

On the harassment report, he gave a one-sentence commitment: “The allegation of sexual harassment will be handled in full accordance with City policy.”

On the conflict-of-interest question, Stockwell pointed to oversight. “The city’s finances are ultimately the responsibility of the city manager who is accountable to the city commission,” he wrote. Anyone suggesting favored treatment toward a department, he added, “simply doesn’t understand the checks and balances built into the systems.”

He also wrote that relationships between colleagues “are neither inappropriate nor unusual in our society.” Six minutes later he sent a clarification: “What I meant to say was ‘co-equal colleagues.’”

The emails did not say who will conduct the harassment review, whether it will be handled inside City Hall or by an outside party, or when it will conclude.

How it ties to our earlier reporting

The Oct. 1 commentary drew on accounts from several city employees over the prior 60 days. They described comments about a coworker’s appearance, a perception that favor shapes how staff are treated, and fear of speaking up.

The letter covers the same ground. It describes a remark about an employee’s appearance that closely resembles one those employees recounted, and the writer says they heard it firsthand. It also describes the same perception of preferential treatment for staff seen as close to top administration.

The letter is not independent proof. It was postmarked two days after the commentary ran, and AlamogordoTownNews cannot determine whether its author is among the employees who spoke to us earlier.

What has changed is the record.

The concerns are now in writing before the commission and Human Resources, they have circulated beyond City Hall, and the city manager has answered them on the record.

What comes next

The mayor and commissioners now have the letter, and the city manager has committed to handling the harassment report under city policy. The next regular City Commission meeting is Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:30 p.m.

Our Oct. 1 commentary called for an independent review of workplace complaints by an outside firm or attorney reporting to the full commission. Whether the commission will take that step is not yet known. The public should demand it and the commission should insist on it and a public report should be made on how to get the city’s house in order which now appears to be running amok. 

The writer’s fear of retaliation is addressed in law. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act makes it illegal to retaliate against an employee who reports harassment or cooperates with an investigation.

This is a developing story.

AlamogordoTownNews will report on any review, its outcome and rather the majority of the commission members act in a manner of professionalism and transparency. The commission should require the city manager to hire an experienced and external legal review of the complaints, policies and recent cultural that had led to these allegations. Stay tuned.

item.title: First-Time Candidates Find Common Ground at Alamogordo Forum
item.description:
LAMOGORDO — Democrats, Republicans and Independents shared a stage at Otero Arts on Tuesday night, and the conversation stayed civil from start to finish.

Alamogordo Town News and KALHRadio.org hosted the nonpartisan candidate forum Oct. 6 as part of their monthly Voices of Alamogordo series. Three candidates for county commission took part, along with candidates for the state Legislature.

The forum came four weeks before the Nov. 3 general election. It gave voters a chance to question the candidates face to face.

Every candidate on stage was running for office for the first time. That put a slate of new faces in front of voters and added a new dimension to this year's election.

Each candidate opened with a statement explaining why they are running. Each then laid out their top priorities for the office they are seeking.

Questions followed from two directions. Audience members submitted a selection, and moderator Chris Edwards added his own. Across party lines, the candidates showed deep passion for their convictions.

Editor's note: add each candidate's name, party and the seat sought.

The Republican candidate told the audience he had been advised not to attend. He came anyway, and said the reception was warm and not what he had been warned to expect.

His remark fit the evening. One line of questioning asked the candidates how residents can get along and bridge the political divide, in the region and across the country. The discussion that followed was civil and positive, and the dialogue stayed warm and friendly throughout.

Organizers had asked for exactly that. The forum announcement said civility and decorum are the standard at Voices of Alamogordo events, for candidates and audience members alike.

Policy questions covered four main areas, among others.

The result was an informative discussion that let voters hear the candidates side by side.

About 47 people attended in person at Otero Arts, 1118 Indiana Ave. The livestream had drawn about 120 views by Wednesday.

The forum is one of many meet-the-candidate events planned across the region this month. Voices of Alamogordo forums are held on the first Tuesday of each month.

The full forum is available on KALH Radio's YouTube channel.

item.title: News and Analysis: Block Sponsored a 2026 Tax Increase on PNM's & Other Utilities Power. State Analysts Said Ratepayers Would Pay
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. —News and Analysis:  Kelly and James Metcalf raise five children on one income. On Sept. 17 they opened a PNM bill for $1,949.26. The same stretch last year cost about $506. Johnny Martin, 74, spent $12,000 on a new air conditioner and appliances and still got four straight bills over $400. 

Residents packed a town hall to tell regulators their bills had doubled or tripled. Regulators blame a meter-reader shortage and a two-stage rate increase.

Rep. John Block was in the room, and regulators praised him for coming. One of his neighbors did not. Tanya Burns told the crowd that Block is seldom around, that he has not responded to her on a number of issues, and that he has not been an advocate for affordable power. She called his appearance political theater weeks before an election. 

Those are her views. The record below is why its important to review rather or not that she has a point.

The bill

Block sponsored House Bill 113 in 2026. It would have taxed electricity generated from renewable resources at 3.75% of its wholesale value, starting Jan. 1, 2027.  A similar bill was filed in 2025. 

In 2025, 57% of PNM's generation came from wind and solar. 

What it would have cost

The Taxation and Revenue Department projected the tax would collect $27.45 million in its first half-year and between $56.5 million and $59.8 million in each of the next three years.  That is more than $200 million collected from renewable generators statewide in three and a half years.

The state's energy department said the tax would increase retail electricity prices for New Mexico ratepayers, that is those very locals already complaining about their PNM Bill last week to the PRC. It was estimated at roughly $3 per megawatt-hour in added cost during peak months of 2024. 

That did not cause the Metcalfs' bill to increase because Block's bill got no where. It was a charge in the wrong direction, every month, while bills are already climbing, sponsored by Block who claims he is there for you the concerned consumer.

The damage beyond the bill

The monthly charge is the smallest part of what the state's analysts warned about.

None of the money would have come back to ratepayers. It was directed to the Severance Tax Permanent Fund.

If the goal was fairness, why raise a tax?

The rate in Block's bill, 3.75%, matches the state's severance tax rate on oil and gas. One state analysis described the bill as taxing renewable energy in a way similar to that tax.  The apparent argument is parity: if oil and gas pay, wind and solar should too.

There are two ways to make two tax rates equal. You can raise the lower one or cut the higher one. Block chose to raise one.

That is a notable choice for this legislator who claims to be a fiscal conservative.  On energy, he filed a tax increase, and it landed on the power source that supplies most of this city's electricity.

This outlet's editorial stance is limited government. A new excise tax, stacked on an existing one, with a $3.5 million bureaucracy to collect it, is not that.

In 2024 Block voted against raising royalty rates on new oil and gas wells on state land. In 2026 he co-sponsored a bill, as its third sponsor, to have combined-cycle natural gas counted as renewable.  So he has opposed higher charges on oil and gas, backed a friendlier label for gas, and proposed a new tax on wind and solar.

None of his 2026 energy bills advanced.  Voters should still ask why the tax was filed twice?

It's been reported in Santa Fe that he is in a race for his life. Per Tanya Burns comments and the analysis that followed it is clearly, why!

Grace Nagamine, the independent on the Nov. 3 ballot, has her specific position on PNM billing and utility costs, are found in videos one her campaign Facebook Page.

Block has declined to speak with Alamogordo Town News, was invited to an upcoming community forum and has not responded.  Written questions about this article, including why he chose a new tax instead of a cut, were sent on 10/5/26 and were not answered by publication. 

ATN will publish his response in full if he provides one.

item.title: Joseph Vazquez Arrested for First Degree Child Abuse
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A 22-year-old Alamogordo man has been arrested and charged with first-degree child abuse after a 1-year-old boy was taken to a hospital with injuries police described as suspicious.

Officers with the Alamogordo Police Department were called to Christus Health Southern New Mexico on Sept. 26 in reference to the child's injuries, the department said in a news release Tuesday. The boy was transported to University Medical Center because of his injuries.

Police said their investigation identified Joseph Vazquez as the suspect. He is charged with abuse of a child resulting in great bodily harm, a first-degree felony, and was booked into the Otero County Detention Center pending a court appearance.

The department did not release details about the child's condition, the nature of the injuries, or Vazquez's relationship to the child.

Police are asking anyone with additional information to come forward. Detectives can be reached at 575-439-4300.

A criminal charge is an accusation. Vazquez is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

item.title: Early voting has begun in Otero County - Alamogordo
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Voters turned out briskly as in-person voting for the 2026 general election opened in Otero County on Tuesday, with early reports showing several hundred ballots already cast in Alamogordo.

The opening-day traffic came through the County Clerk’s sub-office in the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., Room 101. It is the county’s only in-person voting site until expanded early voting begins Oct. 17.

By the close of business, several ballots had been cast, according to.

Candidates spent Tuesday night pushing for exactly that kind of start. At a community forum, Liam Griffin, candidate for NM Senate and Grace Nagamine, an independent running for state House District 51, were among those who urged supporters to get to the polls during early voting rather than wait for Election Day.

Tuesday was also the day the clerk’s office began mailing absentee ballots, and the last day to register to vote by mail or online. Residents who missed that deadline can still register or update their registration in person at any early voting location through Election Day, Nov. 3.

The ballot is topped by races for governor and U.S. Senate, along with congressional, legislative and local offices.

Voting options widen later this month, with early voting sites opening in Alamogordo, Mescalero and Chaparral and one-day mobile stops in Tularosa and Cloudcroft.

Where to vote

In-person absentee voting continues at the County Clerk’s sub-office in the County Administration Building, 1101 New York Ave., Room 101, in Alamogordo. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday through Oct. 30, and 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31.

Early voting at the Otero County Fairgrounds, 401 Fairgrounds Road in Alamogordo, runs Oct. 17 through Oct. 31. Hours are 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday.

Mobile voting comes to the Tularosa Public Safety Facility, 609 St. Francis Drive, on Saturday, Oct. 17, and to Cloudcroft High School, 10 Swallow Place, on Saturday, Oct. 24. Both run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

In Mescalero, early voting is offered at the Inn of the Mountain Gods, 287 Carrizo Canyon Road, from Wednesday, Oct. 28, through Friday, Oct. 30. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

In Chaparral, the Far South Fire Station, 827 Luna St., is open Thursday, Oct. 29, through Saturday, Oct. 31, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Key dates

The last day to request an absentee ballot is Oct. 20. Early and in-person absentee voting end Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3.

Voters can check their registration or apply for an absentee ballot at NMVote.org.
